q: Molecules in a substance are formed by joining atoms together, and there are attractive and ____ forces that arise between the molecules.
e: Both attractive and repulsive forces determine the equilibrium distance between molecules.

q: These forces are known as ____ forces, which are responsible for most of the physical and chemical properties of matter.
e: Intermolecular forces dictate boiling points, melting points, and solubility.

q: A covalent bond within a molecule is described as a pair of electrons ____ between the atoms.
e: Intramolecular covalent bonds rely on the sharing of electron pairs.

q: If the atoms are not identical, the electrons will not be ____ shared.
e: Differences in electronegativity cause unequal sharing of electrons in a bond.

q: The atom with the greater share of the electrons will be slightly ____ and the other atom will be slightly positive.
e: Electrons carry a negative charge, so a greater share results in a partial negative charge.

q: This is known as bond ____.
e: Bond polarity arises from the unequal distribution of electron density.

q: Thus, bond polarity within a molecule results in a ____ of charge over the molecule.
e: Charge separation creates distinct positive and negative poles within the molecule.

q: Moreover, a ____ of the molecule can be expressed numerically by taking into account the magnitude of the charge and the distance separating the charges.
e: Dipole moment is the quantitative measure of molecular polarity.

q: Depending on the difference in ____ between two bonded atoms, covalent bonds can be polar or non-polar.
e: Electronegativity difference is the primary determinant of bond polarity.

q: If two different non-metal atoms are bonded, then the atom with the ____ electronegativity will attract the shared electron pair more strongly.
e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electron cloud closer to its nucleus.

q: The bond becomes more polar as the difference in electronegativity values of the atoms in a covalent bond ____.
e: A larger electronegativity gap leads to greater unequal sharing and higher polarity.

q: In a covalent bond formed between two similar non-metal atoms, the shared electron pair is ____ attracted to the two atoms resulting in a non-polar covalent bond.
e: Identical atoms have the same electronegativity, resulting in perfectly equal sharing.

q: As a result of the dipole formed in a polar covalent bond, the bond possesses the ____.
e: Every polar bond has an associated bond dipole moment.

q: The direction of arrow points to the ____ end of the dipole.
e: By convention in chemistry, the dipole arrow points toward the more electronegative atom.

q: However, any non-polar covalent bond has a ____ dipole moment.
e: Perfectly equal sharing means there is no charge separation, hence a dipole moment of zero.

q: All diatomic molecules containing polar covalent bonds are ____ molecules since they have dipole moments.
e: With only two atoms, a polar bond guarantees the entire molecule is polar.

q: In the case of polyatomic molecules, their dipole moments depend not only on the individual bond dipoles but also on the ____ of the molecules.
e: Molecular geometry determines whether individual bond dipoles cancel out or add together.

q: In such cases, the dipole moment of a molecule is the ____ sum of the dipole moments of various bonds.
e: Dipole moments have both magnitude and direction, requiring vector addition.

q: For example, the $H_2O$ molecule has a ____ shape.
e: The two lone pairs on oxygen force the $H_2O$ molecule into a bent geometry.

q: It is a ____ molecule.
e: The bent shape prevents the O-H bond dipoles from canceling, making water highly polar.

q: In the case of the $CO_2$ molecule, it is ____ and the two polar bonds are arranged symmetrically.
e: Carbon dioxide has no lone pairs on the central carbon, resulting in a 180° linear shape.

q: The two equal bond dipoles point in ____ directions and cancel the effect of each other.
e: In a linear symmetric molecule, the equal and opposite vectors sum to zero.

q: Thus, the dipole moment of $CO_2$ is ____, and it is a non-polar molecule.
e: Despite having polar bonds, the overall symmetry makes the $CO_2$ molecule non-polar.

q: Intermolecular forces are forces that act between a molecule and another ____.
e: These forces govern interactions between distinct molecular entities.

q: It can be classified as van der Waals forces and ____ bonding.
e: Hydrogen bonding is a specific, unusually strong type of dipole-dipole interaction.

q: Van der Waals forces are weak forces which include dipole-dipole interaction, ion-dipole interaction, and ____ dispersion forces.
e: London dispersion forces are present in all atoms and molecules.

q: Dipole-dipole interactions are formed when two ____ molecules interact with each other in space.
e: Permanent dipoles align so that the positive end of one attracts the negative end of another.

q: When this occurs, the partially negative portion of one of the polar molecules is attracted to the partially ____ portion of the second polar molecule.
e: Electrostatic attraction occurs between opposite partial charges on adjacent molecules.

q: This type of intermolecular force is formed from the interaction between an ____ and a dipole molecule.
e: Ion-dipole forces are crucial for the dissolution of ionic compounds in polar solvents.

q: It happens especially in solutions where a negative ion will be attracted to the ____ pole of the polar molecule while a positive ion will be attracted to the negative pole of the polar molecule.
e: Anions are solvated by the partially positive ends of solvent molecules like water.

q: The weakest intermolecular forces that can be formed between atoms, as well as non-polar molecules, are known as ____ dispersion forces.
e: London forces are the only intermolecular forces available to hold non-polar substances together.

q: Because of the constant motion of the electrons, an atom can develop ____ (instantaneous) dipole when the electrons are distributed unsymmetrically about the nucleus.
e: Random electron fluctuations create fleeting dipoles even in non-polar atoms.

q: Then, this instantaneous dipole of the first atom can ____ a second atom to be distorted because electrons repel one another.
e: A temporary dipole alters the electron distribution of neighboring atoms, inducing a matching dipole.

q: It leads to form a dipole in the second atom resulting in an ____ attraction between these two atoms.
e: The attraction between the induced dipoles is fundamentally electrostatic.

q: This electrostatic attraction is known as the London dispersion force, also called ____ dipole-induced dipole interaction.
e: The interaction relies on one dipole inducing the formation of another.

q: These London dispersion forces can occur between ____ molecules such as halogens, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, methane, and noble gases.
e: Substances with no permanent dipole rely entirely on London dispersion forces.

q: Due to these weak attractive forces, non-polar substances can ____ into liquids and can freeze into solids when the temperature is lowered sufficiently.
e: Lowering temperature reduces kinetic energy, allowing weak dispersion forces to hold molecules together as liquids.

q: Hence, London dispersion forces are ____ dipole-dipole interactions that exist between all atoms and molecules.
e: They arise from fleeting, instantaneous fluctuations in electron density.

q: The formation of hydrogen bonds between covalent molecules requires: (1) the first molecule has hydrogen attached to a high ____ atom (F, O, or N).
e: High electronegativity creates a very strong dipole, leaving the hydrogen highly electron-deficient.

q: ...and (2) the second molecule possesses a ____ pair of electrons on a small electronegative atom (F, O, or N).
e: The lone pair on the adjacent molecule acts as the electron donor for the hydrogen bond.

q: Because of the highly electronegativity difference between H atom and bonded F, O, or N atom, the bond is very highly ____.
e: The extreme polarity of the H-F, H-O, or H-N bond is a prerequisite for hydrogen bonding.

q: Hydrogen bonding can occur as both intermolecular and ____ forces.
e: Hydrogen bonds can form between different parts of the same large molecule, like DNA or proteins.

q: A hydrogen bond is a special type of dipole-dipole interaction that occurs between polar molecules and is ____ than van der Waals forces.
e: Hydrogen bonds are significantly stronger than ordinary dipole-dipole or dispersion forces.

q: The hydrogen bond is weaker than a covalent bond and is the ____ of all intermolecular forces.
e: Among all intermolecular forces, hydrogen bonds require the most energy to break.
